## Why `glmap`?

Traditional R mapping packages built on `Leaflet.js` serialize spatial objects into GeoJSON text inside HTML and draw features using DOM/SVG/2D Canvas. When your dataset reaches **100,000 to 1,000,000+ features** or uses high-resolution `terra` rasters, R spends tens of seconds converting coordinates to text and the browser tab freezes.

`glmap` eliminates the JSON and DOM bottlenecks entirely:

1. **C++17 Binary Packing (`GEXP` & `GEXR`)**: Coordinates, polygon `mapbox/earcut` triangle indices (with full interior hole support), and `Float32` raster bands are packed into contiguous binary buffers in milliseconds.
2. **WebGL2 GPU Shaders**: Points, lines, polygons, heatmaps, hexagonal bins, and floating-point rasters are rendered directly on the GPU at 60 FPS.
3. **Zero-Recompute Raster Exploration**: `terra::SpatRaster` layers are uploaded as `Float32` textures. Changing palettes (`viridis`, `magma`, `turbo`, `terrain`, `rdylbu`) or toggling real-time GPU hillshading happens in **0 ms** in the fragment shader.

---

## 1. Instant One-Line Exploration

`glmap()` inspects your input (`sf`, `sfc`, `terra::SpatRaster`, `terra::SpatVector`, `wk::xy`, `nanoarrow`, `data.frame`, or `crosstalk::SharedData`) and automatically chooses the right GPU layer:

```{r}
library(glmap)

# Generate synthetic benchmark data
bench <- gl_benchmark_data(n_points = 100000L, n_polygons = 2000L)

# Instant GPU map of 100,000 points
glmap(bench$points_df, color = ~intensity, palette = "turbo", radius = 3)

# Instant GPU map of a Float32 DEM raster with real-time hillshading
glmap(bench$raster_mat, palette = "terrain", hillshade = TRUE)
```

---

## 2. Building Multi-Layer GPU Maps with Pipes (`|>`)

Use `glmap()` with `add_raster()`, `add_polygons()`, `add_lines()`, `add_points()`, `add_hexbin()`, `add_heatmap()`, and `add_labels()`:

```{r}
glmap(basemap = "dark") |>
  add_raster(
    bench$raster_mat,
    palette = "terrain",
    hillshade = TRUE,
    opacity = 0.65,
    group = "Terrain DEM (Float32)"
  ) |>
  add_polygons(
    bench$polygons_sf,
    fill_color = ~elevation,
    palette = "viridis",
    fill_opacity = 0.65,
    group = "Polygons (C++ Earcut)"
  ) |>
  add_hexbin(
    bench$points_df,
    hex_radius = 0.035,
    palette = "plasma",
    opacity = 0.75,
    group = "Hexbins (C++ 64-bit Hash)"
  ) |>
  add_points(
    bench$points_df,
    color = ~intensity,
    palette = "turbo",
    radius = 3.0,
    opacity = 0.85,
    group = "Points (WebGL2 SDF)"
  ) |>
  use_plugin("export_png")
```

---

## 3. Handling 1M–10M+ Features with In-Memory C++ Spatial Indexing or DuckDB

For massive datasets in interactive R or Shiny sessions, enable `dynamic_viewport = TRUE`, `transport = "server"`, or `add_duckdb()`. `glmap` builds an in-memory C++ spatial index (`gl_spatial_index()`) or queries DuckDB to stream only the features inside the current viewport with automatic Level-of-Detail (LOD) stride sampling:

```{r}
big_df <- data.frame(
  lon = runif(1e6, -75, -71),
  lat = runif(1e6, 45, 48),
  val = rnorm(1e6)
)

glmap(basemap = "dark", transport = "server") |>
  add_points(
    big_df,
    color = ~val,
    palette = "viridis",
    radius = 2.5,
    dynamic_viewport = TRUE
  )
```
